newsitem.title: USA: Clinton signs aid to Everglades, water project law.
newsitem.headline: Clinton signs aid to Everglades, water project law.

text.p: President Clinton signed into a law Saturday a bill that would speed up restoration of the Florida Everglades after years of encroachment by development and solidify the federal role in the work.

The bill authorized $275 million for work in the Everglades out of $4.6 billion for flood control and water development nationwide. Local governments would be required to pay a larger share of project costs.
Clinton also announced during a bill-signing ceremony at the White House that he would sign a bill to create or improve more than 100 national parks and historic sites.

"While we have much further to go, today we move closer to making sure that the Everglades are everlasting," Vice President Al Gore said during the ceremony, which was made part of Clinton's weekly radio speech.

The Everglades, called the "River of Grass," slowly drain water from South Florida, starting near Lake Okeechobee in the south central part of the state, into Florida Bay at the southern tip of the state.
Preservationists say development has cut into its size and distorted its water supply so it gets too much water during winter and too little during summer.

Runoff from farmland and other developed areas carry nutrients that encourage the growth of cattails that crowd out natural grasses in the Everglades, environmentalists say. They say three or four acres of Everglades are lost to cattails each day and put the blame on a tripling of sugar acreage in the past couple of decades.
"That encroachment ... sent the Everglades into a nosedive," Robin Rorapaugh of Save Our Everglades said.

Like the White House, environmentalists hailed the signing of the water bill as an early step in a long process of restoring the Everglades. They said the federal commitment increased the need for Florida voters to approve in November a one-cent a pound levy on sugar grown in Florida.
"It will pass," said Stuart Strahl of the National Audubon Society. "There is a large majority in support of it now."

The so-called sugar tax would collect $900 million over 20 years. It is strongly opposed by the sugar industry, located mostly on the northern edge of the Everglades, and by labor unions worried the tax will destroy jobs.

Under the newly signed water bill, a July 1999 deadline was set for developing a master plan for restoration. The bill also allows some restoration work to go ahead in the interim and formalized a federal, state and local task force to suggest steps in the restoration process.

So far, top priorities are the creation of an area in the Everglade Agricultural Area to hold storm water and restore water quality and the purchase of land for a buffer between the Everglades and urbanized areas on its eastern side.
The cost of Everglades restoration has been pegged at $4 billion.
The Clinton administration endorsed the one-cent sugar tax in February. Critics in Congress said the White House acted too late to get the idea into budget or farm policy bills.
Instead, the farm bill provided $200 million for Everglades restoration and allowed the sale or swap of $100 million in federal land for land in the Everglades.
